# Why is my backtest lying?

*You'll need passive orders and fills (chapter 2), the fair value (chapter 3), why making earns (chapter 4) and adverse
selection (chapter 5).*

## The story

In Prosperity 4 a team that calls itself Kayzerjali tuned one product, Pepper Root, in a backtester. Over one window of
100,000 timestamps the backtest said +2,415; the live platform, on the same window, said +436 (*their claim*). They
didn't conclude that the strategy was bad. They concluded that the backtester's fill model "diverges severely from the
live platform", and rebuilt their loop around it: the live result became the only thing they optimised, and the
backtester became a check for bugs before an upload
[(`references/online-snapshots/Kayzerjali_Prosperity2026/run_cycle.md:3-7`)]{.src}.

A Prosperity 3 team, Frankfurt Hedgehogs, said the same thing more politely. The open-source backtester they used,
Jasper's, was "very accurate and highly flexible", but it "could not … accurately model potential fill probabilities
after inserting liquidity for assets like Rainforest Resin and Kelp"
[(`references/prosperity3-frankfurt-hedgehogs/README.md:898-900`)]{.src}.

Both teams hit the same wall, and it is not a bug in anyone's code. It is a question that recorded data cannot answer.
This chapter is about that question: what a replay has to assume, how much each assumption is worth, and how to work
when you can't know which one is true.

## The idea

### The question a replay can't answer

A backtest replays a recorded day: every tick's order book and every trade that printed. Our bot reads each tick and
sends orders, and the engine decides what would have happened to them. Some of that is easy. An order that crosses the
book, buying at or above the best ask, trades with orders that were really there, at their prices: a *take*, and the
replay knows the answer.

A market maker's income comes mostly from orders that don't cross, *passive* orders waiting for someone to trade with
them. When the recording shows a trade at our bid's price, would it have traded with us? The recording can't say,
because we weren't there. That trade happened between two other bots. Had we been there, the seller might have hit us
instead, or the other bot first, or not traded at all because our order changed the book it saw.

So every backtest engine answers the question by assumption, and the assumption is a setting. Ours has four main ones
(@fig-fill-modes):

- **`all`** (the default, which matches the open-source Prosperity backtester): a recorded trade at our price, or
  through it, fills us.
- **`worse`**: only a trade strictly through our price fills us. If someone sold below our bid, they would surely have
  sold to us first.
- **`none`**: no recorded trades at all; only orders in the visible book fill us.
- **`resting`**: orders stay in the book between ticks and wait in a queue behind the orders already at their price.

![The template on Prosperity 3's round 1, all three days, under each fill model. Resting uses the default queue
(`back`). Data: `data/fill_modes.csv`, from `arena.backtest python/bots/template.py 1 --data p3` in each
mode.](figures/f09_fill_modes.png){#fig-fill-modes
fig-alt="Bar chart of profit over three days under four fill models: all 72,674, worse 63,302, none 28,217, resting 66,558."}

The bot is the same, and so are the days. The answer goes from 28,217 credits to 72,674. More than half of the default
comes from fills that only exist if bots which traded with each other would have traded with us instead
[(`README.md`, "Fill assumptions matter")]{.src}.

### What the market offers at each distance

The replay's assumption can be taken apart, because one half of it is in the data. For a quote at distance d from
the fair, the recording says how often a trade printed at d or beyond, and how many lots: that is what the market
offered a quote there, before any queue or rival. What it can't say is whether those lots would have come to us.

@fig-fill-curve measures that offer on Kelp. A quote at the wall mid sees a print at or beyond it on 13.9% of ticks, a
side; at 1.5 ticks out, 8.0%; at 2 ticks, only 2.4%. Multiply the lots by the edge each one earns and you get what a
quote at each distance could earn, under each rule. Under `all`, every print *at* the quote counts, and the best
distance is 1.5 ticks: 0.44 credits a side a tick. Under `worse`, only prints *beyond* the quote count, and at 1.5 ticks
most of those vanish, since the prints at 1.5 outnumber those beyond it more than two to one. The best distance
becomes 1 tick, at 0.29
[(`data/fill_curve.csv`, from `experiments.day.fill_curve --data p3 --days 1 --products KELP`)]{.src}.

![What a quote at each distance from the wall mid could fill and earn on Prosperity 3's Kelp, before any queue or
rival: left, how often a print reaches it; right, its edge earned per side per tick under each rule. Data:
`data/fill_curve.csv`, from `experiments.day.fill_curve`.](figures/g15_fill_curve.png){#fig-fill-curve
fig-alt="Left: the chance of a print at or beyond a quote falls from 13.9 percent at the wall mid to 8 percent at 1.5 ticks and 2.4 percent at 2. Right: under the optimistic rule a quote earns most at 1.5 ticks, 0.44 credits a side a tick; under the strict rule most at 1 tick, 0.29, and only 0.14 at 1.5."}

That is the whole mechanism in one chart. The further out a quote sits, the larger the share of its fills that are
the doubtful kind, trades printed exactly at its price between other bots. A rule that counts them rewards moving
out; a rule that doesn't punishes it.

### Why the error isn't noise

So the fill model isn't a small, random error. It is biased, and the bias depends on the very parameter you tune. The
backtests say the same as the curve. The table gives the template's PnL with three settings of Kelp's `make_edge`, on
Prosperity 3's round 1 and on three days of round 5 the choice never saw, in thousands of credits.

| `make_edge` | 0.5 | 1 | 1.5 |
|---|---|---|---|
| under `all` | 72.7 | 81.3 | 84.5 |
| under `worse` | 63.3 | 57.8 | 52.3 |
| out of sample (round 5), `all` | 53.9 | 61.2 | 64.6 |
| out of sample (round 5), `worse` | 48.8 | 44.2 | 38.8 |

::: {.content-visible when-format="audio"}
On round 1, a wider quote makes more under the optimistic rule, 72.7 thousand at half a tick up to 84.5 thousand at one
and a half, and less under the strict rule, 63.3 down to 52.3. On three days of round 5 that the choice never saw, the
same happens: 53.9 up to 64.6 under the optimistic rule, 48.8 down to 38.8 under the strict one.
:::

Under `all`, the wider quote wins; under `worse`, it loses; and each rule ranks the edges the same way out of sample as
in sample [(`IDEAS.md`, "Why the zoo beat the template head to head")]{.src}. Held-out data can't settle it, because
the held-out days are replayed under the same assumption. **The fill model decides the edge.** A permutation test
agrees: shuffling the order of Kelp's ticks finds the same best edge and the same lift over the median setting (a
p-value of 0.55 for the best cell, 0.80 for its lift), so the choice comes from each tick's book and the fill rule, not
from anything the price does over time [(`IDEAS.md`, "A permutation test of the whole search")]{.src}.

### Where we stand in the queue

When orders rest, a second assumption joins the first: our place in the queue. A new order joins the back of its
price level. As orders ahead of it trade or are cancelled, it moves up. Trades are visible in the data; cancellations
aren't, only the level shrinking. So the engine must guess where each unexplained drop happened, ahead of us or behind.
Its three answers are `back` (always behind us, the pessimistic default), `front` (everyone else re-posts behind us
every tick) and `prob`, which splits the drops by our place:

::: {.eq speak="a cancellation lands ahead of us with probability equal to the share of the level that is ahead of us, raised to the power N"}
$$\Pr(\text{a cancellation is ahead of us}) = \left(\frac{\text{volume ahead of us}}{\text{volume at the level}}\right)^{N}$$
:::

with N the `--queue-power`, 1 by default (`python/arena/engine.py`; the rule comes from the hftbacktest library). On
Prosperity's round 1 the three hardly differ: 66,558 credits with `back`, 66,562 with `prob`, 67,070 with `front`
[(`data/queues.csv`)]{.src}. That is a fact about Prosperity's book, whose levels are redrawn almost every tick, so
there is rarely a place in a queue to hold (`arena.diagnose`'s `kept` column, 8% on Prosperity; `ON_THE_DAY.md`,
"Which backtest settings match the playground?"). On a book whose levels persist, the three models diverge, and only
the real exchange's fills can choose between them.

### The other things a replay assumes

Each of these is a setting in our engine, each was measured on Prosperity data or a rehearsal, and none can be read
from the data itself.

**When an order arrives.** The replay matches an order against the book the bot saw. If the exchange applies it a tick
later, the price has moved. One tick late, the template on round 1 falls from 72,674 credits to 40,472 under `all`, and
from 63,302 to 31,218 under `worse`; two ticks late, to 36,336 and 28,014 (@fig-delay). Resin's takes against its fixed
fair arrive after the price has already come back. Part of the loss is a race against the limit: a late order is
checked again on arrival, against a position its own earlier orders have moved, and one failure rejects every order for
the product; one tick late, that happened on 3,248 of day 0's 10,000 ticks. Capping each quote's size at 15 to 20 lots
recovers part of it: 45,534 under `all` one tick late
[(`IDEAS.md`, "Orders that arrive a tick late")]{.src}.

![The template with its orders arriving on time, one tick late and two ticks late, under both fill models. Data:
`data/delay.csv`, from `arena.backtest ... --delay N`.](figures/g16_delay.png){#fig-delay
fig-alt="Bar chart: on time 72.7 thousand under all and 63.3 thousand under worse; one tick late 40.5 and 31.2 thousand; two ticks late 36.3 and 28.0 thousand."}

**Whether what we take stays gone.** A replay usually restores the recorded book every tick, so the volume we bought
is back for sale a tick later. In our first rehearsal the bot made 42,446, in that round's units, on the hidden days
with the book restored, and 31,172 when what it took stayed gone: a quarter of the score from one assumption
[(`IDEAS.md`, "The kickoff prompts on a disguised round"; `--deplete`)]{.src}.

**How much of each trade we could get.** If others' hidden orders share every trade with us, we get only a part of
what prints at our price. `--fill-ratio 0.5` halves the available liquidity: the template on round 1 then makes 40,184
credits per tick instead of 72,674 [(`README.md`, "Fill assumptions matter")]{.src}. The Varde rehearsal's exchange did
exactly this, giving resting orders half of each print, unannounced; chapter 12 tells how calibrate came closest with
this setting and still refused.

**Whether orders rest, on a market that jumps.** With orders that live one tick, plain market making on the jumpy
basket legs of Prosperity 2 and 3 earned a few thousand credits each. Let the same quotes rest, and the next snapshot
jumps straight through them, filling them at their own stale price: Prosperity 2's Roses lost 1,477 thousand credits,
having bought and sold 114 thousand units that way on one day
[(`IDEAS.md`, "Market making on products that jump, with resting orders")]{.src}.

**What the position is worth at the end.** A bot that ends the day holding something is scored on cash plus that
position at some price, [$\text{PnL} = \text{cash} + \text{position} \times \text{mark}$]{speak="profit is the cash plus the position valued at the mark"},
and the engine chooses the mark. `--mark` picks the mid, the touch or the last trade. The Varde rehearsal used the
volume-weighted average of the last 100 trades and didn't say so
[(`python/experiments/mock_round/round4/README.md`)]{.src}; the engine has no such mark.

### What to do about it

Three habits follow, and the repo is built around them.

1. **Never trust one fill model.** Run every comparison under at least two, `all` and `worse`, and believe only what
   wins under both [(`README.md`, "Fill assumptions matter")]{.src}. If the ranking flips, the gain is a property of the
   assumption.
2. **Measure the real exchange early.** One upload of a plain bot tells you how far the portal is from each of your
   settings, and its fills file can be read with the same fill curve as above, to measure our share of what the market
   offered (chapter 12).
3. **Prefer the edges a replay can see.** A take against the visible book is filled the same way under every fill
   rule, though not under every delay; income from passive fills is the part to doubt.

::: {.callout-note title="What would differ on another market"}
On ABIDES, where informed traders move the price after their trades, every rule loses and they lie further apart:
−21,798 cents under `all`, −57,872 under `worse`, −362,428 resting with the `prob` queue (chapter 5). On the Varde Exchange, the
closest of our settings on fills was `all` with half of each print. The order of the rules' optimism is the same
everywhere; how far apart they are is not.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="If you know ML"}
A backtest is a simulator, and the fill model is its sim-to-real gap. Two things make it worse than the usual gap.
It is *one-sided*: optimistic fills always look better, so a search drifts toward whatever the simulator flatters. And
it is *correlated with the parameters*: `make_edge` decides what share of your fills are the doubtful kind, so tuning
it is tuning to the gap. Held-out days don't help, as they would against overfitting, because they share the
simulator. The fix is the one for any simulator: measure it against the real system, and treat what remains as a
range, here the span between `all` and `worse`.
:::

  (`python/arena/engine.py`; `ARCHITECTURE.md`, "Matching rules (Prosperity semantics)").

- Bouchaud et al., *Trades, Quotes and Prices*, ch. 21 §21.3–21.4 (PDF pp. 413–421): limit against market orders, the
  value of a place in the queue, and why backtests with phantom orders are biased.
- DeLise, *The negative drift of a limit order fill* (28 pp.): why the fills you get are, on average, the ones you
  wouldn't have wanted, and which fill rule a backtester should therefore use.
:::
